question: Which statement best describes Custom Elements?
options: Custom elements have reaction callbacks: connectedCallback (added to the DOM — set up DOM/listeners here), disconnectedCallback (removed — clean up), attributeChangedCallback (a watched attribute changed), and adoptedCallback (moved to a new document). Declare a static observedAttributes array to choose which attributes trigger attributeChangedCallback.

<template> holds inert markup that isn't rendered until cloned, making it ideal for a component's reusable structure. Inside a shadow root, <slot> is a placeholder where the element's light-DOM children are projected, enabling composition: consumers pass content that the component arranges. Named slots route specific children to specific places.

customElements.define('my-tag', MyClass) registers a class (extending HTMLElement) as a new element. Custom element names must contain a hyphen (my-card) so they never collide with current or future built-in tags. Once defined, you can use <my-tag> in HTML or create it with document.createElement, and it behaves like a first-class element.

element.attachShadow({ mode: 'open' }) creates a shadowRoot — a separate DOM subtree whose markup and styles are encapsulated. Styles inside don't leak out and outside CSS doesn't leak in (except inherited properties and explicit custom properties), so a component's internals are isolated from the rest of the page.

'open' is the common choice — 'closed' offers weak hiding (the reference still exists inside) and complicates testing and accessibility tooling.

Early Web Components included HTML Imports (<link rel="import">) for packaging templates, but that spec was deprecated and removed in favor of ES modules. Today components are shipped as JS modules. Custom elements interop with frameworks: most pass attributes/text fine, but properties and events need care — React (pre-19) historically passed everything as attributes, so libraries or refs were used to set properties and bind events.
